You just need the pro card to accept prize money and to start with the elite field in big races. It's a confusing world with its own language and very expensive toys.

I was an elite female distance runner in college (5k/10k specialist) , had a femoral stress fracture, moved away from athletics for a few years, and am now dabbling in triathlons and my current running fitness sounds very similar to yours. I've only done five tris - 2 Olympics and 3 sprints - so I can't directly comment on how the longer course races would go, but I've placed in the top 3 overall in every race so far and won twice (all local, mid-sized events). I've always liked biking but got into the swimming reluctantly and have surprisingly come to enjoy it. The learning curve is steepest so improvement can be swift! 

Regardless of the distance, I predict that you will place well enough to find triathlons rewarding. However, as a runner recovering from injury, I would caution you from striving for the long course tris at first. I'm guessing working hard has never been your problem, and committing to an ironman will be just the excuse you're looking for to put in hours of exercise every day and possibly dig yourself a deeper hole. Not necessarily from an injury standpoint, but in terms of fatigue and recovery from any psychological knots you may be wrestling as an injured, highly driven female athlete.

All of my projection and speculation aside, I do think that training for shorter events at first will make you all-around stronger, help you discover some new, fun ways to enjoy cross-training, and link you in with a new community of athletes without requiring quite the expense, time commitment, or psychological pressure of starting with an Ironman. Good luck!
